questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a 5 week history of headaches. They are worst on waking and are made worse by coughing and straining at stool. He has vomited most mornings this week and his wife says he has become forgetful. He smoked 40 cigarettes a day for 45 years. Fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen optic discs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Raised intracranial pressure from a space-occupying lesion
questions.e: Morning headaches worse on coughing with vomiting and bilateral papilloedema are classic raised ICP; a heavy smoker suggests a space-occupying lesion such as a metastasis. Tension and cluster headaches never cause papilloedema.

steps.x: Morning headache worse on straining, vomiting and papilloedema in a heavy smoker: raised ICP, likely from a tumour (primary or lung metastasis).

elim: Short, severe unilateral orbital attacks with autonomic features, not morning headache with papilloedema.
Temporal headache with jaw claudication and scalp tenderness; it does not cause bilateral swollen discs.
Daily headache from frequent analgesia; no vomiting, cognitive change or papilloedema.
Band-like, featureless headache; never causes papilloedema or vomiting.

steps.x: D: Raised intracranial pressure from a space-occupying lesion. Morning headache + worse on straining + papilloedema = raised ICP until proven otherwise; think SOL.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has a 2 month history of headaches and, for the last week, horizontal double vision that is worse when looking into the distance. Her BMI is 39 kg/m². On examination there is bilateral papilloedema and she cannot move her left eye outwards beyond the midline. The other eye movements are normal.
questions.q: Which cranial nerve is most likely to be affected?
questions.e: The abducens (6th) nerve supplies lateral rectus; its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to raised ICP, causing horizontal diplopia and failed abduction. A 3rd nerve palsy gives a down-and-out eye with ptosis.

clues: cannot move her left eye outwards
steps.x: Failure of abduction with horizontal diplopia in a patient with papilloedema.

elim: Supplies the muscles of facial expression, not eye movement.
Palsy gives a down-and-out eye with ptosis and often a dilated pupil, not isolated failure of abduction.
Affects vision and the pupil light reflex, not eye movement or diplopia.
Causes vertical diplopia, worse looking down (e.g. on stairs), not horizontal diplopia with failed abduction.

steps.x: A: Left abducens nerve. The 6th nerve has a long intracranial course and is stretched by raised ICP: a false localising sign.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is on the stroke unit with a large right cerebellar haemorrhage. Over 2 hours his GCS falls from 13/15 to 8/15. His observations are shown (see item resources). His breathing has become irregular with pauses.

visual.title: Observations over 2 hours
visual.caption: Systolic BP rising with a widening pulse pressure while the pulse falls.

questions.q: What do these observations most likely indicate?
o: Impending brain herniation from severely raised intracranial pressure
questions.e: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad) are a late physiological response to severely raised ICP and signal imminent herniation and a poor prognosis. Neurogenic shock gives hypotension, not hypertension.

steps.x: Rising BP with widening pulse pressure, falling pulse and irregular breathing: Cushing's triad.

elim: Occurs in spinal cord injury above T6 with a noxious trigger below the lesion, not after a cerebellar bleed with falling GCS.
Rising BP alone does not explain bradycardia, irregular breathing and a falling GCS in an intracranial bleed.
Causes hypotension with bradycardia after high spinal cord injury, not hypertension.
An intrinsic conduction disorder; it does not cause rising BP, irregular breathing and coma.

steps.x: C: Impending brain herniation from severely raised intracranial pressure. Cushing's triad is a late sign of severe raised ICP and warns of herniation; it carries a poor prognosis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 3 month history of daily headaches, a whooshing noise in both ears in time with her pulse, and brief greying-out of her vision when she stands up. Her BMI is 42 kg/m². Neurological examination is normal apart from bilateral papilloedema. CT head and CT venography are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects young women with a high BMI, causing headache, pulsatile tinnitus and visual disturbance with papilloedema and normal imaging. Venous sinus thrombosis must be excluded first, which the normal venography does.

steps.x: Young woman with high BMI, pulsatile tinnitus, visual obscurations and papilloedema with normal imaging.

elim: Can mimic this exactly, but the normal CT venography makes it unlikely.
Causes episodic vertigo, low-frequency hearing loss and tinnitus, but not papilloedema or visual obscurations.
Aura is a gradually spreading visual disturbance before the headache; it does not cause papilloedema.
Usually causes a bitemporal hemianopia and would be seen on imaging.

steps.x: B: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Young woman + high BMI + papilloedema + normal imaging (venous sinus thrombosis excluded) = IIH.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man is admitted with 10 days of worsening headache and vomiting. A junior doctor performs a lumbar puncture before any imaging, for suspected meningitis. Thirty minutes later he becomes unresponsive with bilateral fixed dilated pupils and then stops breathing. A later CT head shows a large frontal tumour with oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
o: Brainstem herniation through the foramen magnum
questions.e: Lumbar puncture in a patient with undiagnosed raised ICP from a space-occupying lesion can precipitate coning through the foramen magnum, which is often fatal; this is why CT comes first.

steps.x: LP done before CT in a patient with an undiagnosed space-occupying lesion, then sudden brainstem failure.

elim: Does not cause sudden respiratory arrest and fixed pupils 30 minutes after an LP in a patient with a tumour.
Gives a postural headache days later, not coma and apnoea within minutes.
Causes back pain and leg weakness, not fixed dilated pupils and apnoea.
Brief loss of consciousness with quick recovery; pupils are not fixed and breathing does not stop.

steps.x: B: Brainstem herniation through the foramen magnum. LP with an undiagnosed SOL creates a pressure gradient and the brainstem cones through the foramen magnum.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted as a child for hydrocephalus. He has a 2 day history of worsening headache, vomiting and drowsiness. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 64 bpm and BP 152/78 mmHg. His GCS is 13/15. There is no neck stiffness or rash.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: Hydrocephalus is a common cause of raised ICP; shunt blockage lets CSF build up, giving headache, vomiting and falling GCS. Without fever or meningism, infection is less likely.

steps.x: Shunt-dependent hydrocephalus with headache, vomiting and reduced GCS, and no signs of infection.

elim: No fever, neck stiffness or rash; the shunt history points to blockage.
Does not cause drowsiness and a falling GCS.
Presents with sudden thunderclap headache, not a 2-day build-up.
Vomiting would not explain headache, drowsiness and reduced GCS.

steps.x: B: Blocked shunt causing hydrocephalus. In a shunted patient, headache plus vomiting plus drowsiness = shunt blockage and raised ICP until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 2 weeks of worsening headache and a low-grade fever after a course of treatment for chronic right otitis media. Today she had a focal seizure affecting her left arm. Her temperature is 38.1°C. There is mild left-sided weakness and bilateral papilloedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her raised intracranial pressure?
questions.e: CNS infection such as an abscess is a cause of raised ICP; spread from chronic otitis media gives fever, focal seizures and focal weakness with papilloedema. Viral meningitis does not cause focal signs.

steps.x: Ear infection spreading to the brain: fever, focal seizure, focal weakness and papilloedema.

elim: Does not cause fever, seizures or focal weakness.
Sudden onset; does not cause fever and 2 weeks of building headache with papilloedema.
Grows slowly without fever and has no link to ear infection.
Causes headache, fever and neck stiffness but not focal seizures, focal weakness or papilloedema.

steps.x: A: Cerebral abscess. Fever + focal signs + raised ICP after ear, sinus or dental infection = cerebral abscess.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man was hit on the side of the head with a cricket ball. He was lucid for an hour, then became drowsy. His GCS is now 6/15 (E1 V1 M4) and his right pupil is dilated and unreactive to light. CT head shows a right-sided biconvex haematoma with midline shift.

visual.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
visual.label: GCS 6
visual.caption: GCS of 8 or less: severe brain injury.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his dilated right pupil?
o: Compression of the right oculomotor nerve by uncal herniation
Direct trauma to the right eye
questions.e: Abnormal pupils in severe raised ICP reflect herniation: the uncus compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, giving a fixed dilated pupil. Horner's syndrome gives a small pupil.

clues: right pupil is dilated and unreactive
steps.x: Expanding extradural haematoma, falling GCS and a fixed dilated pupil on the same side.

elim: A blow to the side of the head with a lucid interval and midline shift points to herniation, not local eye injury.
Causes a small (constricted) pupil with ptosis, not a dilated one.
Gives a relative afferent pupillary defect; the pupil still constricts to light in the other eye.
Causes failed abduction, not a dilated pupil.

steps.x: A: Compression of the right oculomotor nerve by uncal herniation. A unilateral fixed dilated pupil in raised ICP means the temporal lobe uncus is herniating and compressing the third nerve.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with known glioblastoma is brought in by ambulance because she is now hard to rouse. She has had worsening morning headaches and vomiting for a week. Her GCS is 9/15 and her breathing is irregular.
questions.q: Which set of observations is most likely?
o: BP 124/78 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm
BP 160/100 mmHg and pulse rate 118 bpm
BP 196/84 mmHg and pulse rate 46 bpm
BP 84/50 mmHg and pulse rate 128 bpm
BP 92/58 mmHg and pulse rate 44 bpm
questions.e: Severe raised ICP causes Cushing's triad: high systolic BP with a widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing. Hypertension with tachycardia is not Cushing's response.

steps.x: Tumour with severe raised ICP: expect Cushing's triad.

elim: Hypotension with tachycardia suggests shock, not raised ICP.
Hypotension with bradycardia is neurogenic shock, not Cushing's response.
Normal observations would not fit a falling GCS with irregular breathing from raised ICP.
Hypertension with tachycardia is a sympathetic surge (e.g. pain), not Cushing's triad, which has bradycardia.

steps.x: C: BP 196/84 mmHg and pulse rate 46 bpm. Cushing's triad: hypertension with a wide pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular breathing.

questions.stem: A 13 year old girl with new type 1 diabetes is being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis. Six hours after starting intravenous fluids and insulin she complains of a severe headache and becomes confused and irritable. Her pulse rate has fallen from 120 bpm to 58 bpm and her BP has risen to 148/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cerebral oedema is a cause of raised ICP and a recognised complication of DKA treatment in young people; bradycardia with rising BP is an early Cushing-type response. Hypoglycaemia causes tachycardia.

clues: Six hours after starting intravenous fluids
steps.x: Child on DKA treatment with headache, confusion, falling pulse and rising BP.

elim: Causes sweating and tachycardia, not bradycardia with rising BP.
Causes weakness and arrhythmias, not headache with Cushing-type observations.
Not suggested by sudden change during treatment and no fever.
Would give tachycardia and deep breathing, not bradycardia with headache and confusion.

steps.x: A: Cerebral oedema. Headache + bradycardia + rising BP during DKA treatment in a child = cerebral oedema raising ICP.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has had headaches for 6 weeks. She works as an accountant and has taken paracetamol most days with little benefit. She asks which features of her headache are worrying. Her BP is 136/82 mmHg. Examination shows bilateral papilloedema and no focal neurological deficit. A CT head is arranged for that day.
questions.q: Which feature of her headache most suggests raised intracranial pressure?
o: Pain around one eye with a watering eye
Throbbing pain preceded by zigzag lines
Worse on standing and relieved by lying flat
Worst on waking and worse on bending forward
questions.e: Raised ICP headaches are worse in the morning and with coughing, straining or bending, because lying flat overnight and Valsalva raise ICP. A headache relieved by lying flat suggests low CSF pressure.

steps.x: Papilloedema means raised ICP; the classic headache matches it.

elim: Typical of tension-type headache.
Typical of cluster headache.
Typical of migraine with aura.
Typical of low CSF pressure headache (e.g. after LP), the opposite of raised ICP.

steps.x: E: Worst on waking and worse on bending forward. Raised ICP headache: morning, worse on coughing, straining, bending and lying flat.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at work. He has never had a seizure before. His wife says that for a month he has had headaches on waking with nausea and has been 'not himself'. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week. His capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. Fundoscopy shows papilloedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Seizures are a presentation of raised ICP; a first seizure in middle age with morning headaches and papilloedema points to a brain tumour. Idiopathic epilepsy does not cause papilloedema.

steps.x: First seizure in middle age with a month of morning headaches and papilloedema.

elim: 6 units a week is too little, and it does not cause papilloedema.
His glucose is normal.
Usually starts in youth and does not cause morning headache or papilloedema.
Causes brief collapse, not a tonic-clonic seizure with papilloedema.

steps.x: B: Brain tumour. New seizure + morning headache + papilloedema in an adult = SOL causing raised ICP.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has a 4 week history of headaches on waking and vomiting before breakfast, which settle later in the day. His teacher says he has become clumsy and unsteady when walking. On examination he has a broad-based gait, past-pointing and bilateral papilloedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Morning headache and vomiting with papilloedema show raised ICP; ataxia and past-pointing localise to the cerebellum, so a posterior fossa tumour obstructing the fourth ventricle is most likely.

clues: headaches on waking and vomiting before breakfast
steps.x: Morning headache and vomiting with papilloedema plus cerebellar signs in a child.

elim: Causes stereotyped vomiting episodes without ataxia or papilloedema.
Does not cause cerebellar signs and is typical of young women with a high BMI.
Does not cause cerebellar signs or papilloedema.
Acute ataxia after infection, without morning headaches, vomiting or papilloedema.

steps.x: E: Posterior fossa tumour causing hydrocephalus. Raised ICP + cerebellar signs in a child = posterior fossa tumour blocking CSF flow.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman had a mastectomy for breast cancer 3 years ago. She has a 3 week history of morning headaches, vomiting and new right arm weakness. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. An urgent CT head is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT head?
o: Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns
questions.e: Cerebral metastases appear on CT as hypodense lesions with surrounding oedema, which causes the raised ICP. Biconvex and crescent-shaped collections are haematomas after trauma.

steps.x: Known cancer with raised ICP features and a focal deficit: cerebral metastasis.

elim: An extradural haematoma after trauma; there is no head injury.
An acute subdural haematoma after trauma.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage with sudden thunderclap headache.
She has focal weakness and features of raised ICP, so a lesion is expected.

steps.x: D: Hypodense lesion with surrounding oedema. On CT, a metastasis is a hypodense lesion with surrounding (vasogenic) oedema.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has 4 weeks of worsening headache and blurred vision. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her BMI is 34 kg/m². Neurological examination is normal apart from bilateral papilloedema. An urgent CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: After a normal CT, MR or CT venography is needed to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (a risk with the pill) before diagnosing IIH. Lumbar puncture with opening pressure comes after this.

steps.x: Papilloedema with a normal CT in a woman on the pill: venous sinus thrombosis must be excluded.

elim: Does not help in headache with papilloedema.
Comes after venous sinus thrombosis has been excluded.
Not relevant without features of a pituitary tumour.
For giant cell arteritis in older adults, not papilloedema in a 33 year old.

steps.x: C: MR venography. After a normal CT, the second step is MR or CT venography to exclude venous outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with a BMI of 44 kg/m² has 2 months of daily headaches and bilateral papilloedema. CT head and MR venography are normal. A lumbar puncture is performed with her lying on her side.
questions.q: Which result would confirm the diagnosis?
o: CSF glucose less than half of plasma glucose
questions.e: Lumbar puncture with a raised opening pressure is the gold standard for raised CSF pressure, confirming IIH once imaging is normal. Xanthochromia indicates subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: Suspected IIH after safe imaging; the LP is to measure pressure.

elim: Suggests bacterial meningitis.
Suggests viral or TB meningitis.
Suggest multiple sclerosis.
Suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: D: Opening pressure of 36 cmH2O. LP opening pressure is the gold standard for raised CSF pressure (normal roughly 10 to 25 cmH2O).

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has 3 days of headache, fever and vomiting. He is drowsy, with a GCS of 12/15, and has a new left pronator drift. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 134/76 mmHg. Blood cultures have been taken and intravenous antibiotics started.
questions.q: Which investigation must be done before a lumbar puncture?
questions.e: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated until CT excludes a space-occupying lesion or raised ICP, because of the risk of herniation. Reduced GCS and a focal deficit make this essential.

steps.x: Reduced GCS and a focal sign: possible raised ICP or mass lesion.

elim: Does not tell you if lumbar puncture is safe.
Not needed before LP and does not show a mass lesion.
Not relevant; the concern is the brain.
Supports bacterial infection but does not show if LP is safe.

steps.x: B: CT head. Focal signs or reduced GCS: CT head first to exclude a mass before LP.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is intubated and ventilated on the neurosurgical ICU after a severe traumatic brain injury. CT head shows diffuse cerebral swelling with no lesion that needs surgery. His GCS before sedation was 5/15. He is sedated, so his GCS can no longer be followed. The team want to target treatment to keep cerebral perfusion pressure adequate.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide ongoing treatment?
questions.e: In a sedated patient with severe TBI, invasive ICP monitoring allows CPP (MAP − ICP) to be calculated and treatment targeted. Lumbar puncture is dangerous with cerebral swelling.

steps.x: Ventilated patient with severe TBI; sedation hides clinical signs.

elim: Dangerous with diffuse swelling and gives only one-off readings.
Detects seizure activity but does not measure ICP.
Shows anatomy but not continuous pressure, and needs transfers.
Gives indirect blood-flow information, not an ICP value for CPP.

steps.x: C: Invasive intracranial pressure monitoring. ICP monitoring is used in ICU or neuro settings; CPP = MAP − ICP needs a measured ICP.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has 2 months of morning headache and a new focal seizure. An urgent CT head shows a 3 cm left frontal mass with surrounding oedema but cannot show its nature. She has no known cancer. She is alert and stable, with a GCS of 15/15. The neurosurgeons want better detail of the lesion before planning treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CT head is the rapid first-line test; MRI brain with contrast then characterises a space-occupying lesion for neurosurgical planning. LP is contraindicated with a mass and oedema.

steps.x: CT has found the lesion; now it needs to be characterised.

elim: Contraindicated with a mass lesion and oedema.
May help find a primary later, but MRI is needed to characterise the brain lesion.
Gives no useful detail of brain lesions.
Adds nothing beyond the first scan.

steps.x: B: MRI brain with contrast. CT first for speed; MRI brain for detail of the lesion.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 2 weeks of headache, worse on coughing, and vomiting. He is confused and has bilateral papilloedema. His temperature is 37.0°C and there is no neck stiffness. A medical student suggests sending CSF for analysis. No imaging has been done.
questions.q: Which investigation is contraindicated at this stage?
questions.e: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with suspected raised ICP until a CT has excluded a space-occupying lesion, because it can cause fatal herniation. CT head is the right first test.

steps.x: Raised ICP features with no imaging yet.

elim: Safe and useful in any confused patient.
This is the correct first-line test.
Safe, routine blood test.
Safe, and hyponatraemia is a cause of confusion.

steps.x: D: Lumbar puncture. Papilloedema without imaging: no LP. CT head first.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation fell and hit her head 2 days ago. She now has a worsening headache, has vomited twice and is drowsy with a GCS of 13/15. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Urgent CT head is first-line in suspected raised ICP, rapidly showing haemorrhage, SOL or hydrocephalus; NICE CG176 also requires CT within 8 hours in anticoagulated head injury, sooner with vomiting or reduced GCS.

steps.x: Anticoagulated head injury with headache, vomiting and reduced GCS: likely intracranial bleed.

elim: Does not show bleeding.
Dangerous before imaging with possible raised ICP.
Slower and less practical in an unstable patient; CT is first-line.
Can show fractures but not intracranial bleeding.

steps.x: E: Urgent non-contrast CT head. First-line: urgent CT head to identify bleeding, SOL or hydrocephalus (NICE CG176 head injury).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is on the neurosurgical ward awaiting surgery for a large subdural haematoma. His GCS is 13/15 and he has a worsening headache. The nurse finds him lying completely flat with his neck turned to one side and a tight cervical collar strap. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step?
o: Left lateral position with legs raised
Lie fully flat with a pillow under the knees
Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees with the neck neutral
questions.e: Head elevation to 30 degrees with the neck neutral improves intracranial venous drainage and is the first step in managing raised ICP. Head-down positioning worsens it.

steps.x: Positioning and neck compression are blocking jugular venous drainage.

elim: Raises ICP by impeding venous drainage.
Does not improve venous drainage from the head.
Lying flat impairs venous drainage and worsens raised ICP.
May drop cerebral perfusion pressure and is not the recommended angle.

steps.x: D: Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees with the neck neutral. First step in raised ICP: head up 30 degrees, neck neutral, nothing tight round the neck.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a large left frontal intracerebral haemorrhage with midline shift on CT. Her GCS has fallen from 12/15 to 9/15. She has been positioned head-up at 30 degrees. Theatre will be ready in 1 hour. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 172/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment while awaiting surgery?
questions.e: IV 20% mannitol is the first-line drug for acutely raised ICP while awaiting definitive treatment; it draws water from the brain into the blood by osmosis. Dexamethasone is for tumour-related oedema.

clues: Theatre will be ready in 1 hour
steps.x: Acutely rising ICP while waiting for definitive surgery.

elim: Hypotonic fluid worsens cerebral oedema.
Reduces vasogenic oedema around tumours, not the mass effect of a haemorrhage.
Not the first-line osmotic agent for raised ICP.
Reduces CSF production slowly; used in IIH, not acute herniation.

steps.x: D: Intravenous mannitol 20%. First-line pharmacological treatment: IV 20% mannitol, an osmotic diuretic, as a bridge to theatre.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with small cell lung cancer has 10 days of morning headache and vomiting. CT head shows three hypodense lesions with extensive surrounding oedema. His GCS is 15/15. He is not on any steroids. The oncology team plan whole-brain radiotherapy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment now?
questions.e: High-dose dexamethasone reduces the vasogenic oedema around brain metastases and is the mainstay for malignancy-related raised ICP. Mannitol is a short-term measure for acute deterioration.

steps.x: Brain metastases with vasogenic oedema in a stable patient.

elim: A short-term bridge in acute deterioration; not the treatment for tumour-related oedema in a stable patient.
Treats seizures, which he does not have.
Too low a dose; dexamethasone is the steroid of choice for cerebral oedema.
Treats bleeding, not vasogenic oedema.

steps.x: A: High-dose dexamethasone. Malignancy-related raised ICP: high-dose dexamethasone to reduce vasogenic oedema.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after a fall from a ladder. His GCS is 6/15 and he has snoring respirations with pooling secretions. His oxygen saturation is 88% breathing air, pulse rate 62 bpm and BP 176/92 mmHg. A CT head has been requested.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Airway support and urgent anaesthetic help for intubation
Immediate CT head before anything else
questions.e: In emergency raised ICP, an ABCDE approach comes first: GCS 6 with snoring and hypoxia needs airway support and intubation by an anaesthetist, as hypoxia and hypercapnia raise ICP further.

steps.x: GCS 6 with an obstructed airway and hypoxia.

elim: Airway and breathing come first; he would go to the scanner unsafe.
Not used in traumatic brain injury.
May be needed later, but a compromised airway is the immediate threat.
Contraindicated and irrelevant to his immediate needs.

steps.x: A: Airway support and urgent anaesthetic help for intubation. ABCDE first: a GCS of 8 or less needs a protected airway; hypoxia and high CO2 worsen ICP.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has 3 days of headache, vomiting and drowsiness. CT head shows a colloid cyst blocking the third ventricle with greatly enlarged lateral ventricles. Her GCS is 12/15 and falling. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 158/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: CSF diversion by external ventricular drain
questions.e: Raised ICP from obstructive hydrocephalus is treated by CSF diversion, such as an external ventricular drain. Lumbar puncture is dangerous in obstructive hydrocephalus.

steps.x: Obstructive hydrocephalus with falling GCS.

elim: Treats vasogenic oedema around tumours, not obstructed CSF flow.
Dangerous in obstructive hydrocephalus; it can cause herniation.
Too slow and does not relieve obstruction.
Only a temporary bridge; the CSF must be drained.

steps.x: A: CSF diversion by external ventricular drain. Hydrocephalus: CSF diversion (external ventricular drain or shunt).

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has 10 days of headache, fever and a focal seizure after a dental abscess. CT head with contrast shows a 4 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe with surrounding oedema. His temperature is 38.4°C and his GCS is 14/15.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A large cerebral abscess raising ICP needs urgent IV antibiotics and neurosurgical drainage. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with a mass lesion.

steps.x: A large brain abscess causing raised ICP.

elim: May reduce oedema but does not treat the infection.
LP is contraindicated with a mass lesion and oedema.
Inadequate for a large brain abscess.
For metastases, not infection.

steps.x: B: Intravenous antibiotics and neurosurgical drainage. Infection/abscess: urgent treatment with IV antibiotics plus neurosurgical drainage.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman is hit on the left temple by a hockey stick. She is lucid for 2 hours, then becomes drowsy with a GCS of 9/15. CT head shows a left biconvex extradural haematoma with midline shift. She has been intubated and given mannitol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Conservative management with repeat CT in 24 hours
Urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the haematoma
questions.e: Raised ICP from an extradural haematoma needs urgent neurosurgical evacuation; mannitol and other measures only buy time. Prolonged hyperventilation risks cerebral ischaemia.

steps.x: Extradural haematoma with mass effect: a surgical emergency.

elim: An expanding extradural with midline shift needs surgery now.
Treats hydrocephalus, not a haematoma.
Not used in traumatic brain injury.
Only a short-term measure; it causes ischaemia if prolonged.

steps.x: E: Urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the haematoma. Bleed: neurosurgical pathway. Mannitol buys time; evacuation is definitive.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has 3 weeks of worsening headache and right-sided weakness. CT head shows a large left parietal mass with oedema and early midline shift. Her GCS is 14/15. She has been given high-dose intravenous dexamethasone.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Raised ICP from a tumour is treated with dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical review for definitive treatment. LP is contraindicated with midline shift.

steps.x: A brain tumour with mass effect, already on steroids.

elim: Unsafe with a mass, oedema and midline shift.
Contraindicated with a mass and midline shift.
Too slow for a mass with midline shift.
Mannitol is a short-term bridge, not ongoing treatment.

steps.x: E: Urgent neurosurgical referral. Tumour: dexamethasone plus neurosurgical review.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a large meningioma found on a scan for dizziness. Old scans show it has grown slowly over many years. She has no headache, vomiting or papilloedema and her GCS is 15/15. Her ICP is normal when measured at surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which her intracranial pressure stayed normal?
o: Displacement of CSF and venous blood out of the skull
questions.e: The Monro-Kellie doctrine: the skull is a rigid fixed volume of brain, blood and CSF, so a slowly growing mass is compensated by displacing CSF and venous blood. The adult skull cannot expand.

steps.x: A slowly growing mass with normal ICP: compensation.

elim: The adult skull is rigid and cannot expand.
Would raise, not lower, ICP.
Would increase intracranial volume.
Lowers cerebral perfusion; it does not compensate for volume.

steps.x: A: Displacement of CSF and venous blood out of the skull. Monro-Kellie: brain + blood + CSF in a fixed box; a new volume pushes CSF and venous blood out.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man is ventilated on ICU after a traumatic brain injury. He is sedated with an intracranial pressure bolt in place. His BP is 105/60 mmHg, so his mean arterial pressure is 75 mmHg, and his intracranial pressure is 30 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is his cerebral perfusion pressure?
questions.e: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals MAP minus ICP, so 75 − 30 = 45 mmHg, which is too low; rising ICP directly reduces cerebral perfusion.

steps.x: MAP 75, ICP 30.

elim: This is his ICP, not the CPP.
This is his MAP; it ignores the ICP.
Adds ICP to MAP instead of subtracting it.
Divides MAP by ICP; CPP is a subtraction.

steps.x: D: 45 mmHg. CPP = MAP − ICP = 75 − 30 = 45 mmHg (low; usual target is at least 60).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with a large intracerebral haemorrhage has a GCS of 7/15. Over an hour his BP rises from 150/80 mmHg to 210/85 mmHg. His pulse rate falls from 80 bpm to 48 bpm and his breathing becomes irregular. He has no history of hypertension and has received no new drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his rising blood pressure?
o: Sympathetic response to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure
questions.e: In Cushing's triad, rising ICP reduces cerebral perfusion, triggering a sympathetic rise in BP to maintain CPP; the baroreceptor reflex then causes bradycardia.

steps.x: Rising BP with widening pulse pressure and bradycardia: Cushing's triad.

elim: Causes the bradycardia, not the rise in BP.
Would also cause tachycardia, not bradycardia.
Too slow and not triggered by raised ICP.
Does not explain a rise within an hour with falling pulse.

steps.x: E: Sympathetic response to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure. Rising ICP reduces CPP, so the body raises BP sympathetically; baroreceptors then slow the heart.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man is ventilated on the neurosurgical ICU after a head injury. Despite head elevation, sedation and mannitol, his ICP rises. The consultant briefly increases his ventilation rate to lower his PaCO2 to 4.5 kPa while theatre is prepared.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which this lowers intracranial pressure?
o: Cerebral vasoconstriction reducing cerebral blood volume
Osmotic removal of water from the brain
Reduced CSF production by the choroid plexus
questions.e: Controlled hyperventilation, a second-line measure in severe cases, lowers arterial CO2, causing cerebral vasoconstriction, reduced cerebral blood volume and a fall in ICP.

steps.x: Controlled hyperventilation lowers CO2.

elim: Low CO2 constricts, not dilates, cerebral vessels.
Not the effect of a low PaCO2.
This is how mannitol works.
This is how acetazolamide works.

steps.x: A: Cerebral vasoconstriction reducing cerebral blood volume. Low PaCO2 constricts cerebral arterioles, so cerebral blood volume and ICP fall.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman on ICU with a traumatic brain injury has had her ICP controlled by hyperventilation with a PaCO2 of 3.5 kPa for 18 hours. A new registrar asks why the consultant wants to stop this and use other measures.
questions.q: Which is the most likely harm of continuing hyperventilation?
o: Raised intracranial pressure from increased CSF
questions.e: Hyperventilation lowers ICP rapidly but only briefly, and prolonged vasoconstriction reduces cerebral blood flow and can cause ischaemia, so it is reserved for emergencies as a bridge.

steps.x: Prolonged, aggressive hyperventilation.

elim: Low CO2 causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
Alkalosis tends to lower potassium.
Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis.
Not the main harm of hyperventilation.

steps.x: A: Cerebral ischaemia from prolonged vasoconstriction. Hyperventilation works fast but is short-lived and can cause ischaemia, so it is for emergencies only.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with a large cerebellar tumour has a lumbar puncture done in error before his CT was reviewed. He had had 3 weeks of morning headache and vomiting. Within minutes he becomes apnoeic with fixed pupils and cannot be resuscitated. At post-mortem the cerebellar tonsils are pushed down through the foramen magnum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his death?
o: Low CSF volume causing brain sagging over days
Pressure gradient between the cranial and spinal compartments
Spinal cord damage from the needle
questions.e: LP with raised ICP from a mass lowers spinal CSF pressure, creating a gradient that pushes the brainstem and cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum (coning), which is often fatal.

steps.x: LP with a mass lesion, then tonsillar herniation.

elim: Meningitis would not cause death within minutes.
Describes intracranial hypotension, not acute coning.
The needle is placed below the end of the cord.
A traumatic tap does not cause coning.

steps.x: C: Pressure gradient between the cranial and spinal compartments. Draining CSF below lowers spinal pressure, so the brain is pushed down through the foramen magnum (coning).

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with a large meningioma and falling GCS is given intravenous 20% mannitol while awaiting theatre. Over the next 2 hours her urinary catheter drains 1.4 litres and her serum osmolality rises from 290 to 318 mOsm/kg.
questions.q: Which best explains how this drug has lowered her intracranial pressure?
o: Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the choroid plexus
Raised plasma osmolality drawing water out of brain tissue
Reduced vasogenic oedema by stabilising capillaries
Removal of CSF from the ventricles
questions.e: Mannitol, an osmotic diuretic, raises plasma osmolality so water moves from brain tissue into the vessels, temporarily reducing brain volume and ICP; the diuresis follows.

steps.x: An osmotic diuretic raising plasma osmolality.

elim: This is how hyperventilation works.
This is how acetazolamide works.
This is how dexamethasone works.
This is what a ventricular drain does.

steps.x: C: Raised plasma osmolality drawing water out of brain tissue. Mannitol stays in the blood and pulls water out of the brain by osmosis; the effect is temporary.
